title: JAX from first principles to working systems

parts.title: Start here
parts.description: Set up your workspace and run one small experiment.

parts.title: Shared foundations
parts.description: Build a mental model of arrays, transformations, state, and learning.

parts.title: Training systems
parts.description: Train, recover, and measure a complete model.

parts.title: Specializations
parts.description: Take the shared ideas into the work you want to do.

phases.title: Setup & first steps
phases.hardware: CPU reference and executable TPU bridge; TPU execution unverified
phases.checkpoint: Explain which device ran your code and reproduce the result in a fresh environment.

lessons.title: Set up your learning workspace
lessons.objective: Download a starter workspace, select its Python environment, run a saved program, and verify one deliberate change.
lessons.exercise: Edit the starter as shown in Step 6: change the array length from 4 to 6 and the expected sum from 6 to 15. Save, rerun, and keep my-first-run.txt plus a note explaining why the result changed.
lessons.evidence: Keep first_experiment.py, my-first-run.txt with package/device output, the environment interpreter path, and a note deriving the change from a sum of 6 to 15. Record a setup error and its repair if you encountered one.
lessons.check: Which evidence lets another learner reproduce your environment?

lessons.title: Meet your arrays and devices
lessons.objective: Create an array, inspect its dtype and device, and explain the result.
lessons.exercise: Compute column sums instead. State the resulting shape before running the code.
lessons.evidence: Keep the labeled table, row/column calculations, centered-data check, array dtype/device report and the failed reshape with its element-count diagnosis.
lessons.check: For an array of shape (2, 3), what shape results from sum(axis=0)?

lessons.title: Practice with four virtual CPU devices
lessons.objective: Start four logical CPU devices, inspect row-sharded and replicated arrays, and diagnose an indivisible batch.
lessons.exercise: Predict and verify the per-device shapes for twelve rows, then demonstrate how replication repairs an indivisible five-row placement without deleting data.
lessons.evidence: Keep package/device reports, global and local shapes, shard index/value tables, NumPy comparisons, changed-shape predictions, and the five-row failure/repair. State that the run uses one host and does not validate TPU performance.
lessons.check: What does a (12,2) global array sharded with P("data",None) over four devices mean?
lessons.hardware: 4 logical CPU devices on one host

lessons.title: Move your experiment to a TPU
lessons.objective: Verify the device of a completed prediction and its independent numerical reference. Run an explicit TPU target path that fails when TPU is unavailable.
lessons.exercise: Predict the effect of replacing the bias by minus one quarter. Run a second compiled prediction on the selected device. Compare against the original prediction plus the expected constant shift and an independent NumPy calculation.
lessons.evidence: Keep separate CPU and TPU reports with requested/observed platform, package versions, completed predictions, NumPy error and changed-bias and row-permutation checks. Until the target command succeeds, TPU execution remains unverified.
lessons.check: The values match NumPy, but the output array is on CPU when the requested platform was TPU. What has been demonstrated?
lessons.hardware: CPU reference; optional existing TPU runtime

phases.description: Run a saved program and explain its environment, array output and device placement. Start on one CPU; logical devices are a later exercise in placement.
phases.learningAdvice: Keep a first-run log that another learner can reproduce.

studyGuide.question: Can someone else reproduce your first result?
studyGuide.why: Start with one saved program and a known answer. The terminal, interpreter and working folder are part of the experiment: a notebook that imports a package is not yet proof that the downloaded script uses the same environment.

readiness.prompt: You saved a script in your course folder, but the terminal reports that the file does not exist. Which observation should you check first?
readiness.answer: Check the terminal’s current folder and the exact filename, including its extension. Then run the environment’s Python explicitly. Reinstalling JAX will not repair a wrong path.

milestones.title: Make one reproducible result
milestones.task: Run the row-sum example as a saved file. Record the Python executable, package versions, backend, input shape and computed sums. Explain why a package version alone cannot identify which interpreter ran the file.

milestones.title: Separate local practice from accelerator execution
milestones.task: Start a fresh process for virtual CPU devices. Compare its device receipt with the ordinary process. Treat the TPU lesson as preparation until you have a receipt from an actual TPU.

transfer.prompt: A colleague gets the right sums but a different device count. Decide whether the arithmetic is wrong and how to compare the runs.
transfer.approach: Compare values and shapes first, then backend, process startup flags and environment. Device enumeration is a runtime property; equal arithmetic does not imply equal hardware or performance.

pitfall.symptom: Import works in a notebook but fails in the terminal.
pitfall.check: Compare interpreter paths before changing packages; launch both from the intended environment.

studyGuide.completion: Keep a saved script, its command and actual output, plus an explanation of one repaired setup error. Use foundation-toolkit stage 1. A screenshot without a rerunnable file is incomplete.
studyGuide.furtherWork: Fresh-machine Windows/Linux/macOS walkthroughs and novice usability sessions remain unverified; accelerator setup needs a separately observed device run.

phases.title: Arrays & pure functions
phases.checkpoint: Predict output shapes and explain why a pure function is easier to transform.

lessons.title: From NumPy to jax.numpy
lessons.objective: Build feature-wise preprocessing with fitted statistics and verify behavior on new and constant data.
lessons.exercise: Foundation · Standardize the original data using its standard deviation plus epsilon 1e-6. Predict the transformed rows and check feature means and scales. Explain why the scale is only approximately one with epsilon.
lessons.evidence: Keep the fitted mean/scale, hand-derived training values, NumPy comparison, constant-feature test, and together-versus-separate new-batch results. Explain why re-fitting on each inference batch changes the problem.
lessons.check: Why does x.mean(axis=0) return two values?

lessons.title: Shapes, broadcasting, and dtypes
lessons.objective: Specify broadcasting contracts and detect silent pairwise-loss and dtype mistakes.
lessons.exercise: Add a different scalar offset to each row using offsets [100., 200.]. Make its shape explicit.
lessons.evidence: Keep an axis sketch, asymmetric offset checks, aligned-versus-pairwise residual arrays, a rejected shape mismatch, and the float32 precision observation. Explain the intended residual contract.
lessons.check: Which offset shape adds one scalar to each row of a (2, 3) batch?

lessons.title: Pure functions and explicit inputs
lessons.objective: Design an explicit parameter/data interface and return new state without mutating old containers.
lessons.exercise: Create new parameters with weight 3 while retaining the original bias. Show that the original parameters still produce the original predictions.
lessons.evidence: Keep both parameter configurations, their known predictions, a container-alias experiment, a non-mutating update, and an evaluation loss checked by hand. Explain which state the caller owns.
lessons.check: What makes predict easier to transform and test?

lessons.title: Immutable updates and indexing
lessons.objective: Implement functional indexed updates and distinguish accumulated contributions from shape-preserving masks.
lessons.exercise: Replace the last two elements with zero in a new array. Keep x unchanged.
lessons.evidence: Keep original and updated arrays, a repeated-index integer reference, the whole-matrix replacement check, and compact-versus-fixed-shape outputs. Explain replacement, accumulation, and name rebinding.
lessons.check: After y = x.at[1].set(20.), what happens to x?

phases.description: Treat every axis as part of a contract. Work through normalization, broadcasting and immutable updates, then diagnose mistakes that still return plausible numbers.
phases.learningAdvice: Draw the input and output shapes before running each change.

studyGuide.question: Can you spot a wrong axis even when the program runs?
studyGuide.why: Array bugs often return plausible numbers. Use unequal dimensions and hand-computed rows so that a successful operation cannot hide a mistaken meaning. Carry that habit into preprocessing and model inputs.

readiness.prompt: A matrix has three observations and two features. You need one mean per feature. Which axis should be reduced, and how many values remain?
readiness.answer: Reduce the observation axis, axis 0. Two feature means remain. Reducing axis 1 instead returns three observation means, which answers a different question.

milestones.title: Write the data contract
milestones.task: Annotate observation and feature axes; calculate one normalized row by hand. Compare a feature bias with an observation bias using unequal dimensions.

milestones.title: Make preprocessing safe to reuse
milestones.task: Pass parameters explicitly, preserve the caller’s arrays and check indexed accumulation separately from replacement. Carry shape, mask and valid-count checks into foundation-toolkit stage 2.

transfer.prompt: Normalize a matrix with a constant feature and one masked observation. What should the constant feature and the mean denominator do?
transfer.approach: Define the constant-feature policy before division, for example a unit fallback scale. Compute statistics only from valid observations; masking the final output alone leaves the fitted statistics contaminated. Reject a feature with no valid observations or declare an explicit policy.

pitfall.symptom: Predictions look reasonable but adding a bias changes the wrong dimension.
pitfall.check: Write the two shapes before broadcasting and test one row and one column independently.

studyGuide.completion: Retain unequal-shape, constant-column and masked-row cases, a NumPy or hand reference, and proof that inputs were unchanged. Explain every axis in the output.
studyGuide.furtherWork: Sparse and ragged inputs need additional contract-focused labs; this phase deliberately teaches fixed dense arrays first.

phases.title: JAX transformations
phases.checkpoint: Compose grad, vmap, and jit; explain what each transformation changes.

lessons.title: Your first gradient
lessons.objective: Explain local sensitivity and the chain rule, then compare analytic, numerical, and automatic derivatives.
lessons.exercise: Foundation · Define f(x) = x³. Derive f′(x), predict the values at −2, 0, and 3, then verify every prediction with JAX. Explain why the zero at x = 0 does not establish a minimum.
lessons.evidence: Keep predictions and analytic derivations at multiple inputs, the finite-difference step/error sweep with dtype, both argnums checks, and the scalar-objective repair. Explain why a zero gradient need not mark a minimum.
lessons.check: At x = 0, jax.grad(lambda x: x ** 3)(0.0) returns zero. What can you conclude?

lessons.title: Losses and value_and_grad
lessons.objective: Derive and audit a scalar loss, its parameter gradient, and stable versus unstable updates.
lessons.exercise: Foundation · Starting from w = 1, calculate the next weight and loss for α = 0.1 and α = 0.3. Verify both. Explain the overshoot using the error multiplier rather than concluding that autodiff is wrong.
lessons.evidence: Keep handwritten loss/gradient arithmetic, checks at three weights, small/large-rate update results, auxiliary residuals, and mean-versus-sum batch-replication results. Explain the update-scale change.
lessons.check: You duplicate every example and keep the same learning rate. What happens to a sum-loss SGD update compared with the original batch?

lessons.title: Batch a function with vmap
lessons.objective: Specify batching axes and connect per-example gradients to a reduced batch objective.
lessons.exercise: Foundation · Compute each prediction gradient with respect to the shared weight. Predict the shape and the derivative of the dot product, then verify against the input batch.
lessons.evidence: Keep the shape contract, loop/vmap/matrix equivalence, row/column layout checks, per-example gradient array, and mean-gradient identity under two target sets. Explain what each gradient shape means.
lessons.check: For B examples and D shared parameters, what shapes do per-example loss gradients and the mean-loss gradient have?

lessons.title: Compile a function with jit
lessons.objective: Validate compiled loss/gradient values and produce a correctly synchronized latency report.
lessons.exercise: Foundation · Compile value_and_grad(loss), check the loss and gradient against both the eager transform and the manual matrix formula, and explain how you would synchronize a benchmark of its two outputs.
lessons.evidence: Keep the independent loss/gradient calculation, backend/shapes/dtype, first-call interval, warmup/repeat policy, median/range samples, and synchronization of every output leaf. State what the benchmark excludes.
lessons.check: Why wait with block_until_ready when timing a computation?

lessons.title: Tracing, static arguments, and recompilation
lessons.objective: Explain the staging boundary and repair configuration versus runtime-control-flow mistakes.
lessons.exercise: Foundation · Extend reduce_values with a static max mode while preserving sum and mean. Reject unknown modes. Verify all three modes on [1, 2, 3] and on [−4, −1, −2].
lessons.evidence: Keep the small jaxpr observation, the expected tracer Boolean error, checks of both repaired branches, all static reduction modes including invalid-mode rejection, and shape/value-change cases. Do not infer compilation counts from timing alone.
lessons.check: A frequently changing runtime scalar controls a branch. What is the most appropriate first repair for a traced Python if?

phases.description: Begin with a scalar function, then differentiate it, batch it and compile it. Compare each transformed result with a simple reference so you can explain what changed.
phases.learningAdvice: Keep eager and transformed outputs plus a deliberately broken assumption.

studyGuide.question: What changes when you differentiate, batch or compile a function?
studyGuide.why: Build one trustworthy scalar calculation before composing transformations. Differentiation changes the quantity, batching adds an axis, and compilation changes execution. Keeping these roles distinct makes later training failures easier to locate.

readiness.prompt: For a squared residual, is the gradient of the average loss the same shape as the stack of per-example gradients?
readiness.answer: No. A stack retains the examples axis; the gradient of the average reduces that axis. Their mean agrees for the same equally weighted differentiable objective.

milestones.title: Establish the derivative
milestones.task: Predict derivatives at several inputs and compare with an analytic calculation. Check that the loss is a scalar before differentiating.

milestones.title: Compose without changing the question
milestones.task: Compare a Python loop, mapped gradients and their compiled version on the same inputs. Change numerical values separately from shapes and static configuration; record tracing and timing as different observations.

transfer.prompt: One minibatch has two examples and another has six. How should you combine their mean gradients?
transfer.approach: Weight each mean gradient by its example count, add the weighted gradients, then divide by eight. An unweighted average gives examples in the smaller batch too much influence. Verify against a gradient over the concatenated batch.

pitfall.symptom: A Python conditional works eagerly but raises a tracer error under jit.
pitfall.check: Identify the data-dependent truth test. Use a JAX control-flow operation with compatible branch outputs; do not mark changing array data static to suppress the symptom.

studyGuide.completion: Use foundation-toolkit stage 3. Keep independent derivatives, batched/compiled parity and one changed signature. Explain why a faster warm call does not measure first-call cost.
studyGuide.furtherWork: Transformation combinations involving nondifferentiable boundaries require further examples; passing smooth fixtures does not validate arbitrary gradients.

phases.title: State, randomness & control flow
phases.checkpoint: Replay the same experiment with saved state and keys; explain the update order.

lessons.title: Random keys without surprises
lessons.objective: Split keys and show reproducibility without accidental key reuse.
lessons.exercise: Split a fresh seed into four keys, then use vmap to draw two normal values from each. Replay from the seed and compare.
lessons.evidence: Keep a key-ownership tree, two-step replay including the final key, the per-ID reorder check, and the broken/repaired repeated-noise loop.
lessons.check: What happens if the same key is used twice for the same random operation?

lessons.title: Pytrees and structured parameters
lessons.objective: Represent parameters and state in a nested structure and transform its leaves.
lessons.exercise: Compute the squared norm of all gradient leaves. Verify it by adding the weight and bias contributions directly.
lessons.evidence: Keep the parameter/gradient tree diagram, hand-derived leaves and update, flatten/unflatten round trip, nested-scale derivative and missing-key repair.
lessons.check: What structure does grad(loss)(params) have?

lessons.title: Compiled loops with lax.scan
lessons.objective: Replace a fixed-length Python loop with scan and compare final states.
lessons.exercise: Make the decay an explicit scalar argument. Differentiate the final value with respect to decay and compare at 0.5 with the analytic derivative 2.75.
lessons.evidence: Keep the labeled carry/output transition, Python-reference trajectory, polynomial derivative, compiled value check and growing-carry failure with a fixed-shape repair.
lessons.check: What must remain consistent across scan steps?

lessons.title: Branches with lax.cond
lessons.objective: Implement a data-dependent branch that works inside a compiled function.
lessons.exercise: Write a compiled function that applies x * 2 when x is positive and x - 2 otherwise. Check positive, negative, and zero inputs.
lessons.evidence: Keep the branch-contract diagram, eager/jit failure and repair, boundary cases, batched values and off-boundary derivatives, and the shape-mismatch diagnosis.
lessons.check: Can one cond branch return a scalar and the other a length-three array?

phases.description: Make randomness, parameters and loop state explicit. Learn how to repeat an experiment without accidentally reusing randomness or mutating a caller’s state.
phases.learningAdvice: Record the state before and after a transition and explain every changed leaf.

studyGuide.question: Have you saved everything needed to determine the next step?
studyGuide.why: A program’s state includes random keys, counters and structured values as well as model parameters. Explicit ownership lets you reproduce a transition, run a batch safely, and later recover an interrupted experiment.

readiness.prompt: Two simulated examples receive the same random key and run the same sampling function. Should you expect independently allocated draws?
readiness.answer: No. The same key and operation replay the same draw in the tested environment. Split or derive distinct keys at the ownership boundary; unequal observed samples alone do not prove independence.

milestones.title: Name and structure the state
milestones.task: Draw the key ownership tree and identify parameter, optimizer and metadata leaves. Check both tree structure and leaf values.

milestones.title: Audit repeated and conditional transitions
milestones.task: Implement a recurrence with fixed carry shapes. Save per-step observations as outputs, compare with a Python loop, then test both conditional branches and their boundary.

transfer.prompt: Resume a simulation halfway through with the saved position but a newly created key. What must you compare to determine whether it is a true continuation?
transfer.approach: Compare the next draw and next state, then the remaining trajectory, against an uninterrupted reference. Restore the original key and counter as well as position. A similar final average is not a continuation check.

pitfall.symptom: A compiled loop fails when its history grows each step.
pitfall.check: Keep carry structure, shapes and dtypes fixed. Return the per-step history through scan outputs.

studyGuide.completion: Use foundation-toolkit stage 4. Save and reload state in a fresh process and verify the next transition and full remaining trajectory, not only the final mean.
studyGuide.furtherWork: Local deterministic state does not establish concurrent-writer or multi-host recovery; the recovery and operations phases extend these boundaries.

phases.title: Math & optimization
phases.checkpoint: Explain prediction geometry and loss assumptions; verify derivatives; diagnose conditioning, curvature and gradient noise; justify an optimizer using held-out evidence.

lessons.title: Vectors, norms, and projections
lessons.objective: Read a dot product geometrically and separate a vector into a projection and an orthogonal residual.
lessons.exercise: Project \(u=(2,-1,2)\) onto \(a=(1,0,1)\). Check the residual by hand first.
lessons.evidence: Keep the hand-computed projection, perpendicular-residual check, rescaling experiment, zero-direction repair and changed-basis calculation.
lessons.check: Does doubling a nonzero direction double the projection onto its line?

lessons.title: Linear algebra and loss intuition
lessons.objective: Connect a matrix-vector product to predictions and a scalar regression loss.
lessons.exercise: Set the bias to zero. Predict each residual and calculate the loss by hand, then compare it with JAX.
lessons.evidence: Keep the row-by-row predictions, analytic weight/bias derivatives, pairwise-broadcast counterexample, and checked-loss rejection/repair. Include the analytic vector-gradient derivation and mean-versus-sum comparison.
lessons.check: What shape should one scalar target per observation have for predictions of shape (n,)?

lessons.title: Least squares, rank, and conditioning
lessons.objective: Fit a linear model with a direct solver and diagnose nonunique or sensitive coefficients.
lessons.exercise: Add a constant bias column to inputs \((-1,0,1)\) and fit targets \((-1,1,3)\). Recover slope \(2\) and bias \(1\).
lessons.evidence: Save the hand solution, residual orthogonality, duplicate-column ambiguity, perturbation table and NumPy comparison.
lessons.check: Can zero training error prove that fitted weights are uniquely determined?

lessons.title: The chain rule, Jacobians, and directions
lessons.objective: Compute a small Jacobian by hand and connect forward sensitivities to reverse-mode gradients.
lessons.exercise: Replace the scalar loss by \(L(x)=f_0(x)+2f_1(x)\). Predict its gradient at \((2,3)\) before using `grad`.
lessons.evidence: Keep the handwritten Jacobian, JVP and VJP checks, adjoint identity, finite-direction check and stop-gradient diagnosis.
lessons.check: Which object does a reverse-mode pullback map to input sensitivity?

lessons.title: Gradient checking and numerical accuracy
lessons.objective: Compare autodiff with finite differences over several step sizes.
lessons.exercise: Check the gradient again at w = [2., -1.]. Explain why this checks a minimum but does not prove correctness everywhere.
lessons.evidence: Save analytic and numerical derivatives, the step-size/error table with dtype, the nonquadratic transfer check, and the omitted-term failure/repair. Add the one-sided slopes showing why a symmetric probe cannot certify differentiability at a kink.
lessons.check: Does passing one gradient check prove a loss implementation is correct for all inputs?

lessons.title: Curvature, Hessians, and learning rates
lessons.objective: Use curvature to explain learning-rate stability, slow directions and why a zero gradient need not be a minimum.
lessons.exercise: For curvatures \((2,8)\), derive the stable interval and check one step at rate \(0.1\) from \((1,1)\).
lessons.evidence: Keep the Hessian and Hessian-vector checks, stable/divergent trajectories, rescaling comparison and saddle counterexample.
lessons.check: A smooth function has zero gradient at a point. What can we conclude?

lessons.title: Write gradient descent yourself
lessons.objective: Fit a regression model using explicit parameter updates.
lessons.exercise: Run ten steps with learning rate 1.1. Predict whether the error contracts before executing; show evidence of divergence.
lessons.evidence: Keep the two hand-computed steps, rate stability derivation, edge/divergent runs, scaled-curvature transfer and uphill-update repair. Include the tiny-update counterexample and explain your stopping criteria.
lessons.check: What makes rate 1.1 unstable for this particular quadratic?

lessons.title: Probability, likelihood, and stable losses
lessons.objective: Derive binary cross-entropy from a probability model and compute it safely from logits.
lessons.exercise: Compute the binary losses for positive labels at probabilities \(0.8\) and \(0.2\), and explain which prediction is better supported.
lessons.evidence: Keep the hand log-loss, analytic gradient, extreme-logit failure/repair, multiclass shift check and empirical-probability calculation.
lessons.check: Why compute binary cross-entropy from logits?

lessons.title: Regularization and honest validation
lessons.objective: Derive a ridge solution, distinguish data loss from penalized loss, and select a penalty using held-out data.
lessons.exercise: For a target slope of \(4\) and penalty \(\lambda=1\), derive the fitted slope and verify its gradient.
lessons.evidence: Keep the ridge gradient/solve comparison, penalty sweep with separate train/validation losses, duplication check and bias-mask repair.
lessons.check: Which loss should select the penalty in this exercise?

lessons.title: Minibatches, expectation, and gradient noise
lessons.objective: Explain an unbiased minibatch gradient and verify how sampling and reduction affect its variance.
lessons.exercise: Enumerate all \(64\) ordered batches of size \(3\). Check their mean and variance against the independent-sampling formula.
lessons.evidence: Keep the exact per-example mean, enumerated batch-variance calculation, uneven-batch repair, PRNG replay and gradient-accumulation check.
lessons.check: When does averaging batch means reproduce the dataset mean?

lessons.title: Optimize with Optax
lessons.objective: Replace the handwritten update with an optimizer and track its state.
lessons.exercise: At the original zero parameters, compare the first Optax SGD update with an explicit tree-map gradient descent step.
lessons.evidence: Save the analytic first update, manual/Optax equivalence, retained/reset momentum comparison, continuation replay and double-subtraction repair. Include the zero-gradient momentum step and explain why retained state still moves the parameter.
lessons.check: What should a training step retain besides updated parameters for a stateful optimizer?

lessons.title: Adam, clipping, and learning-rate schedules
lessons.objective: Explain Adam’s moments, inspect clipping and schedule order, and compare optimizers with a controlled update budget.
lessons.exercise: Compare global norm clipping with coordinate-wise clipping on \((3,4)\). Check which preserves the ratio of the coordinates.
lessons.evidence: Keep two hand-checked Adam steps, clipping-direction checks, schedule values and boundary, equal-budget loss traces, and the optimization decision memo.
lessons.check: Does clipping gradients before Adam guarantee that final updates obey the same norm threshold?

phases.description: Connect geometry and probability to the updates in a training loop. Begin with linear algebra, gradient checks and gradient descent, then investigate conditioning, curvature, likelihoods, regularization and optimizer behavior.
phases.learningAdvice: For the initial regression project, focus on Linear algebra and loss intuition, Gradient checking and numerical accuracy, Write gradient descent yourself, and Optimize with Optax. The other eight lessons deepen the mathematical explanation; return to them as needed.
phases.projectNote: Complete the regression audit after the four core lessons. This deeper project follows all twelve optimization lessons and connects curvature, conditioning, gradient noise, optimizer state and regularization.

studyGuide.question: Can you explain an optimizer’s behavior from the objective and data?
studyGuide.why: Use a model small enough to solve independently. Connect residuals, gradients, curvature and update state before comparing optimizer names. A lower training loss is useful evidence, but it does not by itself establish better held-out predictions.

readiness.prompt: A model predicts one value for each observation. Targets accidentally have an extra trailing singleton axis. Why might mean squared error still run?
readiness.answer: Broadcasting can construct a pairwise residual matrix instead of one residual per observation. Assert identical prediction and target shapes, then compute one residual by hand before reducing.

milestones.title: Audit the objective and derivative
milestones.task: Work through vectors, residuals, rank and directional derivatives. Use a linear solve and a finite-difference sweep as independent checks.

milestones.title: Connect dynamics to evaluation
milestones.task: Predict a stable versus divergent quadratic update, inspect stable likelihood arithmetic and separate fitting, validation selection and final test reporting.

milestones.title: Make optimizer comparisons fair
milestones.task: Count-weight unequal batches, preserve optimizer moments and schedule position, then change feature scale while retaining the prediction contract.

transfer.prompt: Rescale one feature by a factor of ten. Is the same learning rate automatically a fair comparison?
transfer.approach: No. The parameterization changes directional curvature. Map coefficients to preserve predictions, verify the objective and compare trajectories under stated rates. Fit preprocessing on training data only; never use test performance to choose the rate.

pitfall.symptom: Gradient descent diverges while all values initially remain finite.
pitfall.check: Check the update sign, loss reduction, feature scales and largest quadratic curvature before trying a different seed.

studyGuide.completion: Complete regression-audit, then optimizer-audit. Keep an analytic reference, stable/unstable trajectories, a resumed optimizer comparison and an untouched final evaluation split.
studyGuide.furtherWork: Constrained, nonsmooth and large-scale stochastic optimization are not covered comprehensively. Current ranking evidence is limited to declared synthetic objectives.

phases.title: Neural network training
phases.hardware: CPU first; accelerator for larger experiments
phases.project: Build and audit a neural classifier
phases.checkpoint: Keep train and evaluation behavior separate and reproduce metrics from a saved configuration.

lessons.title: Build a tiny multilayer perceptron
lessons.objective: Implement a small model with explicit parameters before adding a model library.
lessons.exercise: Complement XOR class labels by negating the output layer; verify logits and predictions on new coordinates. Diagnose pairwise loss broadcasting.
lessons.evidence: Keep the 33-parameter shape calculation, independent NumPy cross-entropy, train and held-out seeds, initial/final loss, nearby held-out accuracy, and one repaired score/label shape failure.
lessons.check: Explain why removing tanh makes two affine layers collapse to a linear XOR boundary, then verify a changed label convention.

lessons.title: Model and state with Flax NNX
lessons.objective: Express a model and inspect the distinction between parameters and other state.
lessons.exercise: Separate nnx.Param and nonparameter state; make an independent copied-state snapshot and diagnose shared-variable mutation.
lessons.evidence: Keep the NumPy forward comparison, count of 13 trainable scalars and one diagnostic counter, counter independence after copying state, and logits for batch size one and five.
lessons.check: Explain why exclusion from Param gradients does not prevent forward state mutation, and demonstrate safe snapshot independence.

lessons.title: A compiled train and evaluation step
lessons.objective: Build train and eval steps and check that evaluation does not update weights.
lessons.exercise: Compile separate training and evaluation functions, replay 80 updates, and reconstruct held-out metrics from equal-size chunks without changing state.
lessons.evidence: Keep pre/post parameter snapshots around evaluation, optimizer step count 80, independent held-out loss and accuracy, complete replay comparison, and a deliberately bad held-out update on an isolated clone.
lessons.check: Identify which weights a pre-update loss describes and prove evaluation changes neither parameters nor optimizer step count.

lessons.title: Train a CNN on a small dataset
lessons.objective: Train a classifier with a fixed data split and report held-out metrics.
lessons.exercise: Verify a convolution patch manually, train the noisy-bar CNN on a fixed split, transfer to 10-by-10 input shapes, and repair NCHW/NHWC confusion.
lessons.evidence: Keep the 8-by-8-to-6-by-6 shape diagram, NumPy patch dot product, seeds 20/21, independent held-out cross-entropy, 24-observation confusion matrix, constant-class baseline, and layout failure repair.
lessons.check: Explain what global spatial mean pooling discards and verify that confusion counts and trace reproduce the reported held-out accuracy.

lessons.title: Debug unstable learning
lessons.objective: Introduce a bad learning rate and diagnose it using loss and gradient evidence.
lessons.exercise: Derive the curvature-dependent stable rate, reproduce an alternating divergent trajectory, and distinguish scaled features and corrupted inputs.
lessons.evidence: Keep the analytic error recurrence, per-step weight/loss/gradient norm for rates 0.1 and 0.3, observed 3.24 loss multiplier, changed-scale comparison, clipping bound, and one repaired nonfinite-input case.
lessons.check: Derive why scaling features and targets by ten changes this squared-loss curvature by 100 without treating that bound as universal.

phases.description: Build the same ideas into small neural networks. Understand hidden layers, parameter state, stable objectives and evaluation before moving to a small image classifier.
phases.learningAdvice: Explain a loss curve together with held-out errors; a lower training loss alone is not sufficient.

studyGuide.question: Did the network learn the task, or exploit an evaluation mistake?
studyGuide.why: Move from explicit matrix operations to stateful modules while preserving independent checks. Learn to distinguish capacity, optimization, data quality and evaluation errors before adding layers.

readiness.prompt: A classifier predicts the majority class on every example and reports high accuracy. What information is missing?
readiness.answer: Class counts and per-class errors are missing. A majority baseline can score highly on imbalanced data while missing every rare example. Inspect the confusion matrix and the denominator for each class.

milestones.title: Connect equations to module state
milestones.task: Check a forward pass and unreduced loss independently, then identify parameter and nonparameter state in the NNX model.

milestones.title: Train and evaluate under separate contracts
milestones.task: Keep held-out examples out of updates, verify evaluation leaves state unchanged and read confusion rows as true-class denominators.

milestones.title: Diagnose one failure at a time
milestones.task: Use recorded input ranges, losses, gradient norms and update sizes to distinguish a scale problem from a data or shape problem.

transfer.prompt: Training loss falls, but recall for a rare class is zero. Write the next three checks before changing the model.
transfer.approach: Inspect class counts and labels; compare a constant predictor and per-class confusion; then inspect score distributions and choose any threshold on validation data. Report final metrics on held-out data without using it to tune the repair.

pitfall.symptom: Evaluation results change even though you did not call an optimizer.
pitfall.check: Compare state snapshots and train/eval flags; stochastic or running-statistic behavior may still be active.

studyGuide.completion: Use mlp-classifier before the larger image harness. Retain independent forward/loss checks, two runs with declared seeds, state-pure evaluation and class-specific failure analysis.
studyGuide.furtherWork: Natural-image dataset ingestion, richer augmentation studies and pretrained vision transfer remain larger follow-up labs; synthetic images do not establish real-photo generalization.

phases.title: Data & checkpoint recovery
phases.hardware: CPU first; TPU for system measurements
phases.project: An interrupted run restored with its full state
phases.checkpoint: Compare resumed and uninterrupted runs under a stated determinism tolerance.

lessons.title: Design an input pipeline
lessons.objective: Build and audit a deterministic batched host pipeline.
lessons.exercise: Pad the final three-label batch to four elements with zero. Show that an unmasked mean differs, then derive the correct masked mean.
lessons.evidence: Keep the exact epoch/example ID order, uneven final-batch sizes, hand-derived masked versus unmasked label mean, changed seed order and duplicate/drop audit.
lessons.check: What information is missing from a model-only checkpoint for mid-epoch recovery?

lessons.title: Load, batch, and checkpoint order with Grain
lessons.objective: Build a Grain source/sampler/batch pipeline and verify its record order.
lessons.exercise: Consume two batches, snapshot, and replay the third batch with a new compatible iterator.
lessons.evidence: Keep Grain sampler configuration and exact example IDs for full and partial batches; save iterator bytes, recreate the loader, and compare the next batch before/after restore. Record the incompatible configuration failure.
lessons.check: What makes a fresh loader resume at the saved next batch?

lessons.title: Save model, optimizer, and random state
lessons.objective: Checkpoint complete training state with Orbax and replay the next update.
lessons.exercise: Advance to step five, save to a new directory, restore and verify step six against uninterrupted execution.
lessons.evidence: Keep Orbax save/wait/restore commands, snapshot step, Adam count/moments, exact PRNG words, numerical next-update replay and the parameter-only restart counterexample.
lessons.check: Which checkpoint supports replaying the next Adam update with stochastic targets?

lessons.title: Recover data position and resume
lessons.objective: Persist model/optimizer/key and Grain iterator position at one boundary.
lessons.exercise: Repeat the protocol after one batch and compare the next five batches through step six. Save to a distinct directory.
lessons.evidence: Keep the committed model/optimizer/key/iterator snapshot, uninterrupted and resumed batch-ID ledger across the epoch boundary, exact keys/counts, declared floating tolerances and inconsistent model-only/reader-only restart failures.
lessons.check: Which evidence supports a consistent restart boundary?

lessons.title: Asynchronous checkpoints and failure boundaries
lessons.objective: Distinguish requested, completed, verified and published checkpoint state. Continue a functional update while an asynchronous writer is alive.
lessons.exercise: Verify and publish the already written second checkpoint. Restore it and compare the next functional transition against the live state. Keep the original snapshot unchanged.
lessons.evidence: Keep the requested/completed/accepted step log, the restored snapshot comparison, interrupted-publication result and surfaced finalization error. Explain why directory presence alone does not establish acceptance.
lessons.check: A new checkpoint directory exists but the completion wait raises an exception. Which recovery decision follows this lesson’s protocol?

lessons.title: Track experiments and lineage with MLflow
lessons.objective: Track, retrieve and compare two JAX experiments using explicit data identity, metric steps and downloaded model artifacts.
lessons.exercise: Add a third, deliberately wrong model artifact and show why the smallest training loss alone is insufficient to select a release.
lessons.evidence: Keep both MLflow run IDs, source/data hashes, complete loss histories, the selection metric and predictions independently recomputed from the downloaded artifact.
lessons.check: A run is tagged champion. What does that establish?

phases.description: Follow examples from the dataset into a training update, then save enough information to reproduce the next update after interruption. Track experiment configuration, data identity and metric histories with MLflow alongside complete checkpoints.
phases.learningAdvice: Compare sample IDs, optimizer memory, random state and losses after restore.
phases.projectNote: This connected project also uses performance and distributed lessons. Work through its prerequisites before the full integration check; return here with the completed evidence.

studyGuide.question: Can an interrupted run make exactly the same next update?
studyGuide.why: Recovery is a contract between data order, model state and publication. Tracking explains which run produced an artifact; a checkpoint supplies the values needed to continue it. Neither replaces the other.

readiness.prompt: The weights restore exactly, but the next loss differs. Which state should you inspect before blaming numerical nondeterminism?
readiness.answer: Compare optimizer moments and count, random keys, data permutation/cursor, preprocessing and configuration. The same weights with a different next batch are a different transition.

milestones.title: Preserve record identity and position
milestones.task: Inspect record IDs through shuffling and batching. State the final-batch policy and save iterator state only at the intended consumption boundary.

milestones.title: Prove a committed continuation
milestones.task: Save complete state, restore in a fresh process and compare future IDs and updates across an epoch boundary. Reject an incomplete or incompatible checkpoint before publishing it.

milestones.title: Connect continuation to lineage
milestones.task: Retrieve an MLflow run and its artifact, compare data/source identities and metric-step conventions, and distinguish a registry selection from active deployment.

transfer.prompt: The checkpoint is valid, but the dataset was reordered without changing its filename. Is the saved cursor sufficient?
transfer.approach: No. The cursor is meaningful relative to a dataset identity and ordering configuration. Verify content/version identity first; reject mismatches rather than silently resuming on different records.

pitfall.symptom: The advertised checkpoint step is newer than the restored state.
pitfall.check: Inspect completion and publication order. An asynchronous save request is not proof that the artifact is durable or restorable.

studyGuide.completion: Use sharded-training recovery stages and the MLflow extension. Keep uninterrupted and restarted trajectories, a corrupt/incompatible rejection, and a retrieved artifact tied to its run.
studyGuide.furtherWork: Network storage failures, concurrent checkpoint writers and true multi-host recovery still need separate failure-injection qualification.

phases.title: Transformers & language models
phases.hardware: CPU for small blocks; TPU or GPU for training experiments
phases.checkpoint: Verify masking, sequence handling, restoration, and generation before comparing speed.

lessons.title: Attention from small pieces
lessons.objective: Implement scaled dot-product attention and test its output shape.
lessons.exercise: Permute the three key/value pairs together, then permute only values. Verify invariance for the paired permutation and a changed result for the mismatched pairing.
lessons.evidence: Save the Q/K/V axis diagram, uniform hand calculation, NumPy nonuniform reference, paired permutation check, and wrong-axis repair.
lessons.check: Which dimension should softmax normalize for one query to combine all key/value pairs?

lessons.title: Masking, tokenization, and sequence packing
lessons.objective: Construct a causal mask and prevent packed sequences from attending across boundaries.
lessons.exercise: Encode abcab with a three-character vocabulary. Create shifted inputs/targets, and a loss-eligibility vector for packed segments [0,0,0,1,1] that excludes a cross-segment next-token target.
lessons.evidence: Keep token/target alignment, the two masks, future perturbation, segment-leakage comparison and all-masked-row repair. Verify that masks and ignored loss positions enforce the same boundaries.
lessons.check: What must a packed causal mask enforce?

lessons.title: A Transformer block and mixed precision
lessons.objective: Build a residual attention block and compare numerical behavior across precision choices.
lessons.exercise: Differentiate the mean squared block output with respect to every projection. Check each gradient leaf’s shape and finite values, then perturb one parameter coordinate and compare a central difference.
lessons.evidence: Keep the architecture diagram, zero-projection identity, causal perturbation, independent normalization, finite-difference coordinate check, precision discrepancy and residual-width repair.
lessons.check: If all projection matrices are zero in this block, what should the output be?

lessons.title: Train, checkpoint, and generate
lessons.objective: Train a tiny causal model, restore it, and generate from a fixed seed.
lessons.exercise: Generate twelve new tokens from prompt bcab. Derive the expected cycle first; verify the string. Explain why success on this periodic example does not establish natural-language performance.
lessons.evidence: Save the target alignment, uniform-loss derivation, training/held-out metrics with corpus limitations, snapshot continuation check, generated cycle and metadata/prompt rejection repairs.
lessons.check: Why is saving only parameters insufficient to replay the next Adam update?

phases.description: Build attention and causal masking from small arrays, then connect tokenization, mixed precision, training and generation.
phases.learningAdvice: Inspect what each token can attend to and count only valid targets in the loss.
phases.projectNote: Begin with token contracts and training. Complete the linked performance and deployment prerequisites before cache, export and profiling checks.

studyGuide.question: Can you prove that a predicted token cannot see its future?
studyGuide.why: Attention is a weighted mixing operation whose axes and masks are testable. Build a causal model from these contracts before interpreting a generated sentence as evidence of learning.

readiness.prompt: A query has equal scores for three allowed keys. What are the attention weights, and what happens if one key is masked?
readiness.answer: The weights are equal thirds. Masking one key leaves equal halves on the two allowed keys and zero on the masked key. Normalize over keys, not queries.

milestones.title: Audit attention and targets
milestones.task: Check one attention row by hand, token/target shifts, padding denominators and segment boundaries. Perturb future tokens and inspect earlier outputs.

milestones.title: Train, resume and decode one small model
milestones.task: Preserve residual shapes and sensitive arithmetic, compare the next resumed update and state the decoding policy. Continue into the text harness for cache/full-prefix parity.

transfer.prompt: Two documents are packed into one sequence. Causal masking passes, but one document still changes the other’s predictions. What is missing?
transfer.approach: Causality only blocks future positions. Require matching segment identities too, align targets within each document, and exclude padding or invalid boundaries from the loss. Test a change to the other document while holding the target document fixed.

pitfall.check: Count permitted keys in every query row. A fully masked softmax needs an explicit invalid-query policy; its output and loss must not become valid training evidence.

studyGuide.completion: Use text-harness stages 1–4. Keep independent attention arithmetic, future-token invariance, resumed Adam state and full-prefix/cache parity with declared precision.
studyGuide.furtherWork: Real-corpus curation, tokenizer tradeoff studies, long-context evaluation and live generative quality need further labs beyond the tiny byte-model harness.

phases.title: Performance diagnosis
phases.hardware: CPU for timing concepts; TPU or GPU for profiling
phases.checkpoint: Separate compilation, execution, input stalls, and synchronization before claiming a speedup.

lessons.title: Benchmark asynchronous work correctly
lessons.objective: Warm up a computation and synchronize results before reporting timing.
lessons.exercise: Repeat the synchronized benchmark with 96 rows, then record an independently checked row-energy workload.
lessons.evidence: Keep benchmark.py, complete observed JSON/sample output, workload shapes/dtypes, numerical tolerance/error, first-call versus warmed boundaries, changed-workload report and repaired timer explanation.
lessons.check: Distinguish call-plus-wait wall time from compiler/kernel time; reproduce a new workload with an independent reference.

lessons.title: Diagnose recompilation and host synchronization
lessons.objective: Find a shape-changing call or host read and connect it to observed overhead.
lessons.exercise: Extend the signature ledger to sixteen values and diagnose a static branch, masked final batch and runtime Python branch.
lessons.evidence: Keep the controlled call ledger, actual trace observations labeled as traces, static/dynamic explanation, observed host-consumption intervals, masked-versus-unmasked counterexample and reproduced/repaired tracing failure.
lessons.check: Explain which argument changes affect specialization; justify masked fixed shapes and host reporting boundaries with numerical evidence.

lessons.title: Read an XProf trace
lessons.objective: Capture an actual warmed CPU trace with named steps. Identify nested intervals and avoid double-counting their durations.
lessons.exercise: Convert every model interval to milliseconds and summarize its minimum, median and maximum. Keep the individual samples and explain why four observations cannot establish a tail-latency service guarantee.
lessons.evidence: Keep the actual XPlane and Perfetto paths, named interval durations and nesting check, units and an interpretation separating injected input delay from completed computation.
lessons.check: A step annotation lasts longer than its model annotation. What can this alone establish?

lessons.title: Reason with HLO and the roofline model
lessons.objective: Locate matrix multiplication and activation in StableHLO. Derive the operation and minimum byte counts for a declared matrix contract.
lessons.exercise: Derive the work and minimum traffic for shapes \((48,24)\) and \((24,12)\). Compare your hand calculation with the contract function and report the hypothetical limiting budget.
lessons.evidence: Keep StableHLO, synchronized CPU samples and independent output parity. Derive the byte/FLOP model and label the roofline peak and bandwidth as hypothetical.
lessons.check: The lowered program contains a dot operation and a roofline model predicts a high ceiling. What is still needed before claiming high accelerator throughput?

lessons.title: Memory, rematerialization, and optimization tradeoffs
lessons.objective: Explain why reverse-mode differentiation needs forward intermediates. Compare ordinary and rematerialized gradients with an independent reverse recurrence.
lessons.exercise: Use the direction \(v=(1,\ldots,1)\) and central differences to independently check a directional derivative of the original objective at the existing input. Compare it with the gradient dot direction and report the perturbation.
lessons.evidence: Keep the plain/rematerialized gradient and HVP comparisons, saved-residual counts, compiler-memory observations and synchronized timings. Explain why fewer residuals do not guarantee lower measured memory.
lessons.check: Rematerialization reduces the number of saved residual descriptions but the compiled temporary-byte estimates are equal. What is the supported conclusion?

phases.description: Measure completed work, inspect a real profiler trace and relate compiler output to memory traffic. Compare rematerialization choices while separating saved residuals, compiler memory estimates and observed latency.
phases.learningAdvice: Keep workload shapes, warm-up policy and synchronized timings with your device report.
phases.projectNote: This connected project also uses performance and distributed lessons. Work through its prerequisites before the full integration check; return here with the completed evidence.

studyGuide.question: What measured evidence identifies the bottleneck?
studyGuide.why: Optimize a verified computation and a named timing boundary. Trace events, compiler estimates and wall-clock samples answer different questions; connect them before proposing a change.

readiness.prompt: A JAX call returns an array handle almost immediately. Does a timer ending there necessarily measure completed computation?
readiness.answer: No. Synchronize the result inside the measured boundary. Report first-call setup separately from warmed execution and keep inputs, dtype and output checks fixed.

milestones.title: Choose a comparable measurement
milestones.task: Record warmup, synchronization and sample distributions. Change shapes and host reads separately so you can identify their effects.

milestones.title: Explain the evidence
milestones.task: Locate one annotated operation in a real trace, distinguish nested from additive time and state the memory level behind a roofline estimate.

milestones.title: Test a tradeoff
milestones.task: Compare rematerialized and ordinary gradients before timing. Distinguish saved residuals, compiler estimates and observed peak memory.

transfer.prompt: A kernel becomes twice as fast but the full step barely changes. What does the result suggest?
transfer.approach: First measure the kernel’s original share of the step. Even eliminating a small component has limited total benefit. Also inspect copies, synchronization and changed compilation; a local kernel timer cannot explain the complete pipeline alone.

pitfall.symptom: A claimed speedup disappears in repeated runs.
pitfall.check: Check equivalent work, compilation reuse, synchronization, sample spread and competing system activity; retain the raw samples.

studyGuide.completion: Use the trace and timing stage of sharded-training. Keep before/after correctness, named measurement boundaries, trace locations and distributions with a justified accept/reject decision.
studyGuide.furtherWork: CPU traces do not characterize TPU/GPU communication or memory. Target traces and sustained workload measurements remain required for accelerator claims.

phases.title: Distributed training
phases.hardware: Logical CPU devices for sharding practice; multi-host work needs a real cluster
phases.checkpoint: Explain partitioning, communication costs, and recovery behavior with measured evidence.

lessons.title: Arrays, meshes, and sharding
lessons.objective: Partition an array over a device mesh and inspect its local shards.
lessons.exercise: Compare row and column layouts of a (12,8) array, and repair a ten-row mean with padding plus an explicit mask.
lessons.evidence: Padding repairs the shape but adds artificial rows. The mask keeps them out of both numerator and denominator. Checking only divisibility would miss this statistical error.
lessons.check: With row sharding, why does a global column sum need results from other devices?
lessons.hardware: 4 logical CPU devices on one host

lessons.title: A sharded training step
lessons.objective: Run a training step with explicit data and parameter placement.
lessons.exercise: Run a changed target/initial-state update, then diagnose the factor-of-four local-mean bug and repair uneven-batch aggregation.
lessons.evidence: Each local gradient already divides by its local count. Summing four equal local means omits division by four. For unequal counts, an unweighted mean also misrepresents examples; sum count-weighted local means and divide by total count.
lessons.check: Four equal-size shards compute local mean gradients. Which aggregation gives the global mean gradient?
lessons.hardware: 4 logical CPU devices on one host

lessons.title: Communication-efficient algorithms
lessons.objective: Compare all-reduce and reduce-scatter against the same independent global gradient. Explain global result shape versus per-device storage.
lessons.exercise: Repeat the gradient comparison after reversing both observation rows and labels and changing the initial weights. Verify every all-reduce and reconstructed local replica, then explain why reversing only the labels changes the problem.
lessons.evidence: Keep global NumPy gradient checks, local shard shapes, lowered collectives, changed-value replicas and complete scatter/gather payload accounting. Separate the idealized ring model from observed CPU timings.
lessons.check: A program replaces all-reduce with reduce-scatter and immediately gathers the full vector again. What does the idealized ring model predict?
lessons.hardware: 4 logical CPU devices; target cluster execution unverified

lessons.title: Resilient distributed training
lessons.objective: Restore a complete training state with explicit target sharding. Compare next sample IDs, optimizer state and losses across an epoch boundary.
lessons.exercise: Extend uninterrupted and restored execution by two additional steps. Verify sample IDs, complete state and every local parameter replica. Explain which comparison would fail if a single replica held a different parameter vector.
lessons.evidence: Keep the checkpoint path, saved/restored full state, subsequent sample IDs and losses through a new epoch. Diagnose missing momentum and a changed shuffle key; state the untested multi-host boundary.
lessons.check: The first resumed batch and update match, but sample IDs differ at the next epoch. Which saved value should you inspect first?
lessons.hardware: 4 logical CPU devices; target cluster execution unverified

phases.description: Partition arrays and training updates, compare all-reduce with reduce-scatter, and restore a complete sharded state across an epoch boundary. Verify CPU placement and arithmetic before separate cluster validation.
phases.learningAdvice: Compare against a single-device reference; measure real accelerator performance separately.
phases.projectNote: This connected project also uses performance and distributed lessons. Work through its prerequisites before the full integration check; return here with the completed evidence.

studyGuide.question: Is the distributed update still optimizing the same objective?
studyGuide.why: Start with the global mathematical operation, then specify ownership and communication. Logical CPU devices help expose placement and reduction mistakes before you spend accelerator time.

readiness.prompt: Two devices see one and three valid examples. Should their mean gradients receive equal weight?
readiness.answer: No. Weight by valid example counts. Sum local gradient numerators and valid counts, then divide once. Padding and empty partitions must not silently change the denominator.

milestones.title: Verify placement and the global update
milestones.task: Inspect actual shard indices and compare each relevant output with an independent unpartitioned calculation, including padded and unequal partitions.

milestones.title: Connect communication and recovery
milestones.task: Inspect collectives without inferring network speed from payload size. Restore data position and optimizer state before comparing subsequent global steps.

transfer.prompt: A final batch leaves one partition empty. Should it contribute a zero mean, be omitted, or fail?
transfer.approach: Do not compute an undefined local mean. Accumulate a zero numerator and zero valid count for the empty partition, reduce globally and reject a globally empty batch. Compare the result with the valid unpartitioned examples.

pitfall.symptom: The gradient grows with device count.
pitfall.check: Check whether local means were summed without count normalization. Verify one complete update before interpreting a training curve.

studyGuide.completion: Use sharded-training. Retain actual placements and collectives, independent uneven/empty-partition checks and full-state replay. Label logical CPU devices explicitly.
studyGuide.furtherWork: Real network collectives, multi-controller ingestion and host-loss recovery are unqualified. The optional launch instructions are preparation, not execution receipts.

phases.title: Scientific computing
phases.hardware: CPU; target accelerator execution requires separate evidence
phases.checkpoint: Recover a known physical parameter and report error, stability, and gradient checks.

lessons.title: A functional physical simulation
lessons.objective: Implement a pure scalar state transition with units and a fixed time grid. Separate a discrete implementation oracle from continuous approximation error.
lessons.exercise: Change the rate to \(0.3\), the initial excess to \(5\), and use twenty steps of \(0.1\) seconds. Verify the full discrete trajectory and bound the endpoint error against the exponential.
lessons.evidence: Full geometric/exponential comparisons, fixed-horizon refinement table, unstable-step failure and repair. Keep the environment, observed outputs and your explanation of the figure.
lessons.check: The code matches the geometric-sequence reference exactly but differs from the exponential. What have we established?

lessons.title: Vectorize trajectories and scan time
lessons.objective: Construct and verify a fourth-order fixed-step transition. Distinguish batch-major from time-major trajectory layouts.
lessons.exercise: Add a fourth initial condition, verify the changed output shape and exponential values, then verify that reordering initial conditions reorders rows only.
lessons.evidence: Polynomial/exponential references, batch/time shape diagram, permutation and final-only checks. Keep the environment, observed outputs and your explanation of the figure.
lessons.check: What does a shape of (3, 41) mean in the batch-major solver?

lessons.title: Differentiate through a solver
lessons.objective: Derive an independent discrete solver sensitivity. Check an observation-loss gradient at a nonoptimal parameter.
lessons.exercise: Change the initial value to \(3\) and the rate to \(0.4\). Verify the endpoint gradient against the continuous derivative, then check the derivative with respect to the initial value as well.
lessons.evidence: Polynomial derivative, finite-difference window, sensitivity refinement and detached-gradient diagnosis. Keep the environment, observed outputs and your explanation of the figure.
lessons.check: An autodiff derivative matches the discrete RK4 formula, but both differ from the exact ODE derivative. What should you test next?

lessons.title: Fit parameters and scale the simulation
lessons.objective: Fit a constrained physical parameter through an executed simulator. Separate training fit, held-out prediction and solver refinement.
lessons.exercise: Repeat inference for a new true rate \(0.4\) using analytically generated observations, starting at \(0.9\). Show that the recovered parameter and held-out predictions change consistently.
lessons.evidence: Full loss/rate histories, held-out and refined-grid metrics, noisy reference search, timing boundary and limitations. Keep the environment, observed outputs and your explanation of the figure.
lessons.check: You fit only observations at time zero and every rate gives zero loss. What is the problem?

phases.description: Build and differentiate a physical simulator, recover a positive rate from observations, and separate numerical accuracy, identifiability and measured execution cost.
phases.learningAdvice: Complete gradients, explicit state and scan first. Start with analytic references, check discretization and sensitivity, then fit parameters and defend held-out predictions.

studyGuide.question: Are you fitting the physical model or the solver’s error?
studyGuide.why: Use an analytic system to separate simulation correctness, numerical discretization and parameter inference. An accurate autodiff derivative can still belong to an inaccurate discretized model.

readiness.prompt: A solver’s output is differentiable. Does that establish that its gradient matches the continuous differential equation?
readiness.answer: No. Autodiff follows the implemented discrete steps. Compare a discrete reference and refine the step size toward an analytic or higher-accuracy continuous reference.

milestones.title: Validate dynamics and axes
milestones.task: Compare one integration step independently, refine the grid and separate independent trajectory axes from dependent time steps.

milestones.title: Fit an identifiable inverse problem
milestones.task: Check objective derivatives, choose observations that constrain the unknown parameter and evaluate predictions at held-out times. Separate noise sensitivity from discretization bias.

transfer.prompt: All observations are taken at the initial time of a decay process. Can they identify its decay rate?
transfer.approach: They identify initial amplitude but contain no elapsed-time decay signal. Collect later observations and inspect parameter sensitivity; more optimizer steps cannot create missing information.

pitfall.symptom: The fitted rate changes as the time step is refined.
pitfall.check: Compare solver error and parameter estimates across resolutions before attributing the shift to physical variation.

studyGuide.completion: Use scientific-inverse. Keep discrete and continuous references, a refinement study, derivative checks, recovered parameters and a held-out/noise sensitivity report.
studyGuide.furtherWork: Adaptive solvers, event handling, stiff systems, PDEs and domain-specific physical validation remain outside the scalar ODE lab.

phases.title: Probabilistic modeling
phases.hardware: CPU; transparent JAX samplers with an optional NumPyro ecosystem bridge
phases.project: A Bayesian model with diagnostic evidence
phases.checkpoint: Report sampler diagnostics and distinguish uncertainty from predictive error.

lessons.title: Distributions and sampling
lessons.objective: Distinguish samples, density, variance and standard error Check normal moments against independent analytic expectations
lessons.exercise: Change the sensor to mean \(-1\), standard deviation \(0.5\), and draw \(30000\) readings from a new key. Predict the variance and the standard error of the sample mean, then verify both moments.
lessons.evidence: Seeded arrays, independent density values, moment discrepancies and underflow diagnosis. Keep the environment, observed outputs and your explanation of the figure.
lessons.check: Which statement explains why a large Monte Carlo sample can have a precise mean while individual readings remain variable?

lessons.title: Build a Bayesian regression
lessons.objective: State the prior, likelihood and observation-noise assumptions Derive posterior precision and check a closed-form special case
lessons.exercise: Strengthen the prior by changing its scale from two to one half. Predict the direction of change in the weight norm and check it. Explain why a tighter posterior need not mean a better model.
lessons.evidence: Precision derivation, exact fractional reference, host solve and predictive variance plot. Keep the environment, observed outputs and your explanation of the figure.
lessons.check: Which variance describes a new noisy reading at a given input?

lessons.title: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and sampler diagnostics
lessons.objective: Implement leapfrog with the correct half-step boundaries Check reversibility and an independent analytic gradient
lessons.exercise: Increase the step size to 1.2 with the same leapfrog count. Record acceptance and positive energy errors. Explain why keeping more rejected samples is not a repair for unstable integration.
lessons.evidence: Reversibility check, four traces, two-dimensional moments, key replay and classical split R-hat with limitations. Keep the environment, observed outputs and your explanation of the figure.
lessons.check: Four chains have classical split R-hat close to one. What can we conclude?

lessons.title: Variational inference and model checking
lessons.objective: Derive the diagonal Gaussian variational optimum for a correlated target Separate optimization error from variational-family error
lessons.exercise: Replace the target correlation by zero and rederive the optimal diagonal variances and minimum KL. Verify that the diagonal family can now represent the target exactly.
lessons.evidence: Analytic and optimized KL, variance comparison, Monte Carlo estimate and explained residual stress fixture. Keep the environment, observed outputs and your explanation of the figure.
lessons.check: The variational mean is correct and the optimization gradient is tiny. Why can posterior intervals still be too narrow?

phases.description: Specify probability models, derive exact Bayesian regression, implement and diagnose HMC, and compare variational approximations with predictive evidence.
phases.learningAdvice: Start with likelihoods, stable losses and explicit random keys. Check a known posterior before trusting a sampler, then separate inference error from model mismatch.

studyGuide.question: Which uncertainty does your model actually represent?
studyGuide.why: Use an exactly solvable Bayesian regression to check inference. Separate uncertainty about weights, uncertainty about a future observation, and mismatch between the assumed likelihood and the data.

readiness.prompt: Should an interval for a new noisy observation equal an interval for the latent mean prediction?
readiness.answer: No. The observation includes additional likelihood noise. Under the independent Gaussian model, add its variance to the latent predictive variance before taking a square root.

milestones.title: Build an exact reference
milestones.task: Keep distribution units and normalization, derive a posterior in a small solvable case and compare latent versus observation uncertainty.

milestones.title: Challenge approximate inference
milestones.task: Compare sampler moments with the exact target, inspect multiple-chain diagnostics and measure the covariance lost by a diagonal approximation. Use predictive residuals to challenge the likelihood itself.

transfer.prompt: Chains agree closely, but prediction residuals bend systematically with the input. What should be changed first?
transfer.approach: Investigate the model’s mean function and observation assumptions. Agreement between chains concerns exploration of the chosen posterior; it does not certify that the chosen model describes the data.

pitfall.symptom: Intervals are narrow and diagnostics look reassuring despite poor predictions.
pitfall.check: Check whether you plotted latent or observation uncertainty, and whether the likelihood or mean function misses structure.

studyGuide.completion: Use bayesian-regression. Retain analytic posterior checks, sampler/approximation diagnostics and a predictive model-mismatch case, with uncertainty assumptions stated.
studyGuide.furtherWork: General hierarchical models and robust modern diagnostic workflows need further examples. The instructional sampler is not a replacement for validated inference libraries.

phases.title: Reinforcement learning
phases.hardware: CPU; target accelerator execution requires separate evidence
phases.project: An evaluated policy in a functional environment
phases.checkpoint: Compare a trained policy to a baseline across several seeds and report variability.

lessons.title: Write a functional environment
lessons.objective: Implement reset and step as pure functions with explicit state. Distinguish termination, time-limit truncation and an absorbing finished state.
lessons.exercise: Begin at position \(0\), choose left for three actions with horizon \(3\), and then attempt one more action. Verify the event flags, total reward and absorbing state.
lessons.evidence: Keep independent transition enumeration, reward/terminal checks and the absorbing-state diagnosis. Explain the state and observation contract.
lessons.check: What should step emit when called on a finished state?

lessons.title: Batch environments and scan rollouts
lessons.objective: Build a scan over vmapped transitions with explicit key ownership. Reconstruct episode returns and reward-to-go from padded trajectories.
lessons.exercise: Change the batch to \(7\) environments and the horizon to \(5\). Verify array shapes, one ending event per episode and zero rewards after finishing.
lessons.evidence: Keep reconstructed trajectories, randomized keys, padding masks and independent return calculations. Show how a changed key affects interaction without changing the environment rules.
lessons.check: Which axis should be summed to obtain one return per environment from a time-major reward array?

lessons.title: Policy gradients and PPO
lessons.objective: Derive and implement the score-function policy gradient for complete episodes. Train with fresh stochastic rollouts and a fixed behavior policy per PPO batch.
lessons.exercise: Run REINFORCE with a different training seed and retain the initial and final exact return. Verify that the final policy improves on the uniform baseline without requiring every intermediate point to improve.
lessons.evidence: Keep the exact small-state policy-gradient comparison, actual training curves and frozen PPO reference quantities. Diagnose changed clipping signs and distinguish Monte Carlo variation from an incorrect objective.
lessons.check: During multiple PPO epochs on one rollout batch, what must remain fixed?

lessons.title: Evaluate agents across seeds
lessons.objective: Separate training seeds, evaluation streams and individual episodes. Report per-agent means and variability with an explicit aggregation unit.
lessons.exercise: Compute the paired held-out improvement over the uniform baseline for each trained agent. Report all \(5\) differences and their mean, keeping the training run as the unit.
lessons.evidence: Keep multiple trained seeds, fixed held-out streams, exact versus sampled returns and failed trajectories. Explain uncertainty and demonstrate evaluation leaves the policy unchanged.
lessons.check: What does evaluating one policy on many episodes fail to measure?

phases.description: Build a functional environment, collect randomized trajectories, train policy-gradient and clipped-policy agents, and evaluate independent seeds.
phases.learningAdvice: Keep terminal and timeout behavior explicit. Verify a small enumerated expectation before trusting a sampled policy gradient, then separate training from held-out evaluation.

studyGuide.question: Is the policy improving under a fixed evaluation protocol?
studyGuide.why: Environment semantics and data collection define the learning problem. Verify transitions, masks and behavior-policy probabilities before trusting a noisy return curve.

readiness.prompt: An episode stops because its time budget expires. Must its bootstrap value be zero?
readiness.answer: Not necessarily. Distinguish truncation from genuine terminal states and state whether the task is finite-horizon or continuing. A timeout alone does not imply that future value is zero.

milestones.title: Test environment and rollout semantics
milestones.task: Check transitions independently, preserve terminal rewards and label time/environment axes. Store the behavior policy that collected each action.

milestones.title: Compare updates and evaluations fairly
milestones.task: Audit the clipped objective for both advantage signs. Freeze the evaluation protocol, compare a simple baseline and distinguish training seeds from repeated episodes.

transfer.prompt: You evaluate one trained agent over many episodes and report a tiny uncertainty interval. Does this measure sensitivity to training randomness?
transfer.approach: No. Those episodes characterize that agent under the evaluation distribution. Train independent agents to assess training variation, retain agent-level means and state the experimental unit.

pitfall.symptom: PPO ratios always equal one after every update.
pitfall.check: Check that old log probabilities were stored at collection rather than recomputed from the current policy.

studyGuide.completion: Use policy-evaluation. Keep independent transition checks, behavior-policy identity, changed-horizon cases and paired evaluations across declared independent training seeds.
studyGuide.furtherWork: Continuous actions, value-function estimation and larger benchmark environments need new implementation and evaluation labs; this tabular task is deliberately bounded.

phases.title: Pallas kernels
phases.hardware: CPU interpretation/simulation reference; TPU target lab requires separately validated hardware
phases.project: A checked Pallas kernel with an explicit target qualification plan
phases.checkpoint: Compare against a reference across shapes and justify each optimization with evidence.

lessons.title: Pallas grids and BlockSpecs
lessons.objective: Implement an actual Pallas Ref-writing kernel with grid and BlockSpecs. Derive block coordinates and distinguish them from element offsets.
lessons.exercise: Test a singleton row and a changed nondivisible matrix with negative values. Verify full NumPy agreement and exact output shapes for two block choices.
lessons.evidence: Independent full-array comparisons, ownership map, tail fixtures and a floor-grid omission diagnosis. Keep the environment, observed outputs and your explanation of the figure.
lessons.check: For block shape (2,4), what does a BlockSpec index map returning (i,j) select?
lessons.hardware: CPU Pallas interpretation; actual TPU lowering and performance unverified

lessons.title: A first TPU kernel
lessons.objective: Implement a real TPU-targeted Pallas launch with a broadcast BlockSpec. Specify target layout and float32 compute/output-cast policies.
